Terrible
tĕr´rĭ-bl
adj. (causing terror; awful; dreadful; rendering Hebrew yare, 'ayom, Greek phoberos)
From Latin terribilis, from terreo, to frighten. In the Authorized Version the word means awe-inspiring rather than of poor quality, and it is applied to God as a title of honour, not of complaint.

Biblical Definition

In the Authorized Version terrible means what inspires terror, and it is applied to God as praise. Moses sings it at the sea: “Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?” (Exodus 15:11), and the Psalms make the terror of His works the reason His enemies submit: “Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee” (Psalm 66:3). Nehemiah shows how naturally the word sits beside covenant faithfulness in prayer: “I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments” (Nehemiah 1:5). The same God is terrible and keeps mercy, and the man praying sets the two side by side without apology. Joel fixes the word to the day of reckoning: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come” (Joel 2:31). Modern English has degraded the word to mean merely bad, which is why readers stumble here; the older sense is nearer to dreadful in its original force — full of dread, and rightly so.

Webster 1828 Definition

Frightful; dreadful; adapted to excite terror; formidable; awful. In Scripture it is a title of honour for God, whose works and whose day are terrible, and never a term of mere disparagement.

expand to see more

TERRIBLE, a. [L. terribilis, from terreo, to frighten.] Frightful; adapted to excite terror; dreadful; formidable.

2. Adapted to impress dread, awe or solemn reverence; as, the terrible majesty of God.

3. Severe; sharp; as, terrible discipline.

TERRIBLENESS, n. The quality or state of being terrible; dreadfulness; formidableness.

TERRIBLY, adv. In a manner to excite terror or fright; dreadfully; violently.

TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; also, the cause of extreme fear.

Key Scripture

Exodus 15:11 — "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?"

Psalm 66:3 — "Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee."

Nehemiah 1:5 — "And said, I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments:"

Joel 2:31 — "The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come."

Modern Corruption

The word has decayed in English until it means only bad, and with the word has gone the thing: a God whose works excite dread is thought incompatible with a God who keeps covenant and mercy.

expand to see more

Language shifts, and doctrine can drain out through the shift without anyone deciding anything. Terrible once meant awe-inspiring; it now means of poor quality, so that a modern ear hearing “the great and terrible God” registers something like an accusation. The loss is not merely lexical. When the vocabulary of dread disappears, the fear of the LORD — which Scripture calls the beginning of knowledge — has no words left to inhabit, and worship contracts to affection. Nehemiah felt no strain in addressing the terrible God who keeps covenant and mercy, and the strain a modern reader feels is a symptom worth naming.

The practical corruption follows: a religion in which God is admired but not feared, and in which Joel's great and terrible day is either allegorized away or quietly dropped from preaching. Scripture will not permit the edit. The same prophets who promise mercy announce the day; the same Moses who sang of steadfast love asked who is like the LORD, fearful in praises. Recover the older sense of the word and the older shape of worship returns with it — reverence and godly fear, in which mercy is precious exactly because the One showing it is terrible in His works.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yare (to fear, to be awed) supplies the participle rendered terrible; 'ayom (dreadful, awesome) and Greek phoberos (fearful, terrible) complete the field.

expand to see more

Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, revere, be awed; its participle is the “terrible” of Nehemiah 1:5 and Psalm 66:3.

Hebrew 'ayom (H366) — dreadful, terrible, awesome; used of an army terrible with banners.

Hebrew yir'ah (H3374) — fear, reverence; the disposition Scripture calls the beginning of wisdom.

Greek phoberos (G5398) — fearful, terrible; used of falling into the hands of the living God.

Greek epiphanes (G2016) — illustrious, notable, glorious; the Septuagint's word in Joel 2:31 for the terrible day.

Usage

"“How terrible art thou in thy works!” — the word is praise, not complaint."

"“The great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy” — dread and covenant mercy sit together."

"“The great and the terrible day of the LORD” — the reckoning is named before it comes."
